In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Back to the Future: Unsupervised Backprop-based Decoding for Counterfactual and Abductive Commonsense Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we perform abductive and counterfactual reasoning with pre-trained language models without supervision, by incorporating both past and future contexts through backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DELOREAN, an unsupervised decoding algorithm that uses backpropagation to incorporate future constraints into left-to-right language models for abductive and counterfactual reasoning.
papers.conclusion: DELOREAN is a general unsupervised method for generative reasoning tasks that can be easily adapted to other tasks.
papers.key_findings:
DELOREAN outperforms all unsupervised baselines on abductive and counterfactual reasoning tasks in automatic and human evaluation.
It achieves competitive coherence with supervised methods while being unsupervised.
The method balances coherence and minimal edits in counterfactual story rewriting.
The ranking step using BERT's next sentence prediction improves performance.
The approach demonstrates that nonmonotonic reasoning can be achieved through conditional decoding without supervision.
papers.abstract: Abductive and counterfactual reasoning, core abilities of everyday human cognition, require reasoning about what might have happened at time t, while conditioning on multiple contexts from the relative past and future. However, simultaneous incorporation of past and future contexts using generative language models (LMs) can be challenging, as they are trained either to condition only on the past context or to perform narrowly scoped text-infilling. In this paper, we propose DeLorean, a new unsupervised decoding algorithm that can flexibly incorporate both the past and future contexts using only off-the-shelf, left-to-right language models and no supervision. The key intuition of our algorithm is incorporating the future through back-propagation, during which, we only update the internal representation of the output while fixing the model parameters. By alternating between forward and backward propagation, DeLorean can decode the output representation that reflects both the left and right contexts. We demonstrate that our approach is general and applicable to two nonmonotonic reasoning tasks: abductive text generation and counterfactual story revision, where DeLorean outperforms a range of unsupervised and some supervised methods, based on automatic and human evaluation.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Humans and language models diverge when predicting repeating text
papers.research_question: How do human and language model memory mechanisms differ in next-word prediction tasks involving repeating text spans?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that human and language model memory mechanisms diverge in repeating text prediction tasks, and shows that adding a recency bias to attention heads can align model performance more closely with human behavior.
papers.conclusion: Humans and GPT-2 show substantial divergence in memory-based next-word prediction, but this can be mitigated by adding a recency bias to attention heads, though at the cost of increased perplexity.
papers.key_findings:
Human and GPT-2 next-word predictions are strongly aligned in the first presentation of a text span but diverge in subsequent presentations when memory plays a role.
The divergence is traced to specific attention heads in middle layers (e.g., layer 6) that exhibit induction behavior, enabling near-perfect recall.
Adding a learned power-law recency bias to attention heads reduces the divergence and improves human-model similarity on repeated spans.
The intervention increases model perplexity on non-repeating text, indicating a trade-off between human-like memory and general next-word prediction performance.
The findings suggest that transformer LMs use different memory mechanisms than humans, challenging their use as models of human cognition.
papers.limitation: The intervention increases model perplexity on non-repeating text, potentially harming general next-word prediction performance.
future_direction: Describing the change in model states during repeated presentations of a stimulus.
Using the model to learn more about human memory.
Developing alternate forms of attention for increased efficiency based on recency biases.
papers.abstract: Language models that are trained on the next-word prediction task have been shown to accurately model human behavior in word prediction and reading speed. In contrast with these findings, we present a scenario in which the performance of humans and LMs diverges. We collected a dataset of human next-word predictions for five stimuli that are formed by repeating spans of text. Human and GPT-2 LM predictions are strongly aligned in the first presentation of a text span, but their performance quickly diverges when memory (or in-context learning) begins to play a role. We traced the cause of this divergence to specific attention heads in a middle layer. Adding a power-law recency bias to these attention heads yielded a model that performs much more similarly to humans. We hope that this scenario will spur future work in bringing LMs closer to human behavior.

papers.title: How Do Neural Sequence Models Generalize? Local and Global Cues for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
papers.research_question: How do neural sequence models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts when local and global context cues conflict?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts by interpolating between local and global context cues, and that noise-based regularization can control this interpolation.
papers.conclusion: Neural sequence models' out-of-distribution generalization can be predicted by a log-linear interpolation of local and global context cues, and the weighting can be controlled by noise-based regularization.
papers.key_findings:
Neural language models' out-of-distribution predictions are well approximated by a log-linear interpolation of local and global context models.
Generalization behavior varies across languages: local context model fits well for regular languages and English, while global context model fits better for Finnish and Chinese.
Noise during training modulates the interpolation: input token substitution encourages global generalization, while hidden state dropout encourages local generalization.
Log-linear interpolation consistently outperforms linear interpolation in predicting model behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows that interpolation behavior arises in regularized log-linear models with separate local and global features.
papers.limitation: The theoretical explanation relies on a feature function that may not realistically represent deep network features, makes strong assumptions about feature predictive power, and becomes vacuous for certain parameter values.
future_direction: Explaining data-dependent aspects of the local-global trade-off, especially cross-linguistic differences.
Determining whether architectural improvements can more effectively target specific kinds of structured generalization.
papers.abstract: After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its behavior be predicted? We show that RNN and transformer language models exhibit structured, consistent generalization in out-of-distribution contexts. We begin by introducing two idealized models of generalization in next-word prediction: a local context model in which generalization is consistent with the last word observed, and a global context model in which generalization is consistent with the global structure of the input. In experiments in English, Finnish, Mandarin, and random regular languages, we demonstrate that neural language models interpolate between these two forms of generalization: their predictions are well-approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global predictive distributions. We then show that, in some languages, noise mediates the two forms of generalization: noise applied to input tokens encourages global generalization, while noise in history representations encourages local generalization. Finally, we offer a preliminary theoretical explanation of these results by proving that the observed interpolation behavior is expected in log-linear models with a particular feature correlation structure. These results help explain the effectiveness of two popular regularization schemes and show that aspects of sequence model generalization can be understood and controlled.

papers.title: Semantic Composition in Visually Grounded Language Models
papers.research_question: This thesis explores whether and how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces multiple methods (WinogroundVQA, Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, Causal Tracing, Syntactic MeanPool, Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization) to probe, analyze, and improve the compositional abilities of visually grounded language models.
papers.conclusion: The work explores the compositionality of visually grounded semantics, introducing methods to probe and improve it, and draws connections to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.
papers.key_findings:
Generative vision-language models like BLIP 2.0 and MiniGPT-4 perform poorly on the compositional WinogroundVQA benchmark.
Syntactic Neural Module Distillation reveals that larger sentence embedding models (GTR-T5) are more compositional, but model size is not the only determining factor.
Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization (CACR) improves relation alignment in vision-language models and outperforms the previous state-of-the-art method (IAIS) on the Winoground benchmark.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, hyperparameter tuning for the SynNaMoN experiments was unfeasible, and the dataset had to be constrained to a subset of trees and production rules.
The choice of linguistic formalism (Penn Treebank) may influence the probing results of compositional structure.
future_direction: Exploring whether different linguistic formalisms are better proxies for a model's compositional structure.
Further work on the causal tracing experiment for image captioning models (implementation in progress).
papers.abstract: What is sentence meaning and its ideal representation? Much of the expressive power of human language derives from semantic composition, the mind's ability to represent meaning hierarchically & relationally over constituents. At the same time, much sentential meaning is outside the text and requires grounding in sensory, motor, and experiential modalities to be adequately learned. Although large language models display considerable compositional ability, recent work shows that visually-grounded language models drastically fail to represent compositional structure. In this thesis, we explore whether & how models compose visually grounded semantics, and how we might improve their ability to do so. Specifically, we introduce 1) WinogroundVQA, a new compositional visual question answering benchmark, 2) Syntactic Neural Module Distillation, a measure of compositional ability in sentence embedding models, 3) Causal Tracing for Image Captioning Models to locate neural representations vital for vision-language composition, 4) Syntactic MeanPool to inject a compositional inductive bias into sentence embeddings, and 5) Cross-modal Attention Congruence Regularization, a self-supervised objective function for vision-language relation alignment. We close by discussing connections of our work to neuroscience, psycholinguistics, formal semantics, and philosophy.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the ability of neural language models to make syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure, and how does structural supervision affect learning outcomes and syntactic invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from few examples, and explicit structural supervision improves both few-shot learning and syntactic invariance across transformations.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of inducing syntactic features from minimal exposure and show some invariance to syntactic transformations, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models show robust few-shot learning for nominal number and verbal argument structure after minimal exposure.
Structurally supervised models (ActionLSTM and RNNG) outperform the LSTM model in most syntactic generalization tests.
Models demonstrate syntactic invariance by transferring generalizations learned in base contexts to transformed contexts.
There is a singular bias for nouns and a transitive bias for verbs in few-shot learning, with models assuming default categories when evidence is sparse.
Accuracy often improves with increased exposure for some tests, particularly for structurally supervised models.
papers.limitation: The small training data size poses limitations and suggests the need for scaling to larger datasets for better generalization.
future_direction: Scaling the carefully-controlled methods to larger data settings.
papers.abstract: Humans can learn structural properties about a word from minimal experience, and deploy their learned syntactic representations uniformly in different grammatical contexts. We assess the ability of modern neural language models to reproduce this behavior in English and evaluate the effect of structural supervision on learning outcomes. First, we assess few-shot learning capabilities by developing controlled experiments that probe models' syntactic nominal number and verbal argument structure generalizations for tokens seen as few as two times during training. Second, we assess invariance properties of learned representation: the ability of a model to transfer syntactic generalizations from a base context (e.g., a simple declarative active-voice sentence) to a transformed context (e.g., an interrogative sentence). We test four models trained on the same dataset: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two LSTM-variants trained with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al.,2016; Charniak et al., 2016). We find that in most cases, the neural models are able to induce the proper syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often from just two examples during training, and that the two structurally supervised models generalize more accurately than the LSTM model. All neural models are able to leverage information learned in base contexts to drive expectations in transformed contexts, indicating that they have learned some invariance properties of syntax.

papers.title: Successor Heads: Recurring, Interpretable Attention Heads In The Wild
papers.research_question: Do recurring, interpretable attention heads (successor heads) exist in large language models, and how do they work?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces successor heads, a class of attention heads that increment tokens in ordinal sequences, and finds that they use abstract mod-10 features across model architectures and scales.
papers.conclusion: Successor heads are a recurring, interpretable component in LLMs that use compositional mod-10 features for incrementation, providing insights into numeric representations and model internals.
papers.key_findings:
Successor heads exist across models from 31M to 12B parameters and across architectures (GPT-2, Pythia, Llama-2).
Successor heads use compositional numeric representations with mod-10 features.
Vector arithmetic with mod-10 features can steer head behavior.
Successor heads are important for low loss on incrementation tasks in natural language data.
Successor heads exhibit polysemanticity (also perform acronym prediction).
papers.limitation:
Mod-10 features do not fully capture the greater-than bias and fail to steer Days and Letters tasks.
The numeric projection might capture more than just the numeric subspace, affecting successor decoding.
future_direction: Future work on how language models represent numeric concepts.
papers.abstract: In this work we present successor heads: attention heads that increment tokens with a natural ordering, such as numbers, months, and days. For example, successor heads increment 'Monday' into 'Tuesday'. We explain the successor head behavior with an approach rooted in mechanistic interpretability, the field that aims to explain how models complete tasks in human-understandable terms. Existing research in this area has found interpretable language model components in small toy models. However, results in toy models have not yet led to insights that explain the internals of frontier models and little is currently understood about the internal operations of large language models. In this paper, we analyze the behavior of successor heads in large language models (LLMs) and find that they implement abstract representations that are common to different architectures. They form in LLMs with as few as 31 million parameters, and at least as many as 12 billion parameters, such as GPT-2, Pythia, and Llama-2. We find a set of 'mod-10 features' that underlie how successor heads increment in LLMs across different architectures and sizes. We perform vector arithmetic with these features to edit head behavior and provide insights into numeric representations within LLMs. Additionally, we study the behavior of successor heads on natural language data, identifying interpretable polysemanticity in a Pythia successor head.

papers.title: Should Neural Network Architecture Reflect Linguistic Structure?
papers.research_question: Should neural network architecture reflect linguistic structure for better language modeling and representation of sentence meanings?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces recurrent neural network grammars (RNNGs) that incorporate hierarchical syntactic structure, showing they outperform sequential and tree-structured RNNs in language generation and downstream semantic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Neural network architectures that reflect linguistic structure, such as RNNGs, are more effective for language modeling and representation.
papers.key_findings:
RNNGs achieve better language generation results compared to models that do not exploit linguistic structure.
Unsupervised learning of syntactic structures using reinforcement learning improves performance on downstream semantic tasks over sequential and tree-structured RNNs.
papers.abstract: I explore the hypothesis that conventional neural network models (e.g., recurrent neural networks) are incorrectly biased for making linguistically sensible generalizations when learning, and that a better class of models is based on architectures that reflect hierarchical structures for which considerable behavioral evidence exists. I focus on the problem of modeling and representing the meanings of sentences. On the generation front, I introduce recurrent neural network grammars (RNNGs), a joint, generative model of phrase-structure trees and sentences. RNNGs operate via a recursive syntactic process reminiscent of probabilistic context-free grammar generation, but decisions are parameterized using RNNs that condition on the entire (top-down, left-to-right) syntactic derivation history, thus relaxing context-free independence assumptions, while retaining a bias toward explaining decisions via "syntactically local" conditioning contexts. Experiments show that RNNGs obtain better results in generating language than models that don't exploit linguistic structure. On the representation front, I explore unsupervised learning of syntactic structures based on distant semantic supervision using a reinforcement-learning algorithm. The learner seeks a syntactic structure that provides a compositional architecture that produces a good representation for a downstream semantic task. Although the inferred structures are quite different from traditional syntactic analyses, the performance on the downstream tasks surpasses that of systems that use sequential RNNs and tree-structured RNNs based on treebank dependencies.

papers.title: Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Do different languages lead LLMs to think differently? Do LLMs internalize the cognitive biases embedded in different languages, specifically in causal reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, and provides empirical evidence that LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases, showing typologically aligned attention patterns and a shared understanding when reasoning succeeds.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit language-specific biases in causal reasoning that impact performance, but when reasoning succeeds, they form a shared understanding that transcends surface linguistic form.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English.
Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese.
When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form.
Attention patterns over syntactic components show consistent layerwise trends but differ in absolute weights between Chinese and English, reflecting language-specific structural biases.
The similarity of layerwise attention patterns (measured by SVCCA) correlates with reasoning accuracy across different input structures and languages.
papers.limitation:
Focuses exclusively on Chinese and English, representing only a small portion of the world's linguistic diversity.
Does not encompass all model architectures or training paradigms.
Primarily focuses on attention patterns and hidden representations; does not incorporate additional interpretability methods.
future_direction: Extending BICAUSE to a broader set of languages.
Advancing research on multilingual interpretability and alignment mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Language is not only a tool for communication but also a medium for human cognition and reasoning. If, as linguistic relativity suggests, the structure of language shapes cognitive patterns, then large language models (LLMs) trained on human language may also internalize the habitual logical structures embedded in different languages. To examine this hypothesis, we introduce BICAUSE, a structured bilingual dataset for causal reasoning, which includes semantically aligned Chinese and English samples in both forward and reversed causal forms. Our study reveals three key findings: (1) LLMs exhibit typologically aligned attention patterns, focusing more on causes and sentence-initial connectives in Chinese, while showing a more balanced distribution in English. (2) Models internalize language-specific preferences for causal word order and often rigidly apply them to atypical inputs, leading to degraded performance, especially in Chinese. (3) When causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages, indicating a shared understanding beyond surface form. Overall, these results suggest that LLMs not only mimic surface linguistic forms but also internalize the reasoning biases shaped by language. Rooted in cognitive linguistic theory, this phenomenon is for the first time empirically verified through structural analysis of model internals.

papers.title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a compact vector representation of an input-output function (function vector) in transformer language models that can be extracted and used to trigger the task in various contexts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that compact vector representations of input-output functions (function vectors) exist in transformer language models and can be extracted via causal mediation analysis; these vectors robustly trigger the corresponding tasks even in zero-shot and natural text contexts.
papers.conclusion: Function vectors are a compact internal representation of functions in large language models that can be extracted and used to trigger tasks robustly across contexts, and they exhibit compositional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors can be extracted from a small set of attention heads via causal mediation analysis.
FVs are portable across different contexts, including zero-shot and natural text settings.
FVs often encode the output vocabulary of the task but contain additional information beyond that.
FVs can be composed via vector algebra to create new function vectors for combined tasks.
The causal effect of FVs is strongest when added to middle layers of the network.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to relatively simple functions.
The conditions under which FVs can be composed are not fully characterized.
The extraction method relies on having a set of exemplars for the task.
future_direction: Investigate more complex functions.
Explore the relationship between FVs and other internal representations.
Use FVs for model editing and control.
papers.abstract: We report the presence of a simple neural mechanism that represents an input-output function as a vector within autoregressive transformer language models (LMs). Using causal mediation analysis on a diverse range of in-context-learning (ICL) tasks, we find that a small number attention heads transport a compact representation of the demonstrated task, which we call a function vector (FV). FVs are robust to changes in context, i.e., they trigger execution of the task on inputs such as zero-shot and natural text settings that do not resemble the ICL contexts from which they are collected. We test FVs across a range of tasks, models, and layers and find strong causal effects across settings in middle layers. We investigate the internal structure of FVs and find while that they often contain information that encodes the output space of the function, this information alone is not sufficient to reconstruct an FV. Finally, we test semantic vector composition in FVs, and find that to some extent they can be summed to create vectors that trigger new complex tasks. Our findings show that compact, causal internal vector representations of function abstractions can be explicitly extracted from LLMs. Our code and data are available at https://functions.baulab.info.

papers.title: Ungrammatical Influences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing
papers.research_question: Do ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing? Specifically, are readers temporarily distracted by coherent but grammatically incompatible local structures during parsing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence from a connectionist model and human reading experiments that ungrammatical local structures can influence parsing, supporting a dynamical, self-organizing approach to language processing.
papers.conclusion: Ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing, and dynamical, self-organizing models like connectionist networks can account for these effects, pointing towards parallel processing solutions to parsing tractability.
papers.key_findings:
A Simple Recurrent Network model shows higher error (Kullback-Leibler Divergence) on sentences containing irrelevant local coherences (e.g., noun-noun compounds) that are grammatically incompatible with the global structure.
Human reading times are slower for sentences containing such ungrammatical local coherences (Experiment 1), indicating distraction by grammatically ruled-out interpretations.
A stronger slowing effect is found for reduced relative clauses with homophonous verbs compared to non-homophonous verbs (Experiment 2), showing the effect extends beyond lexical compounds.
The results suggest that parsing involves competition among local coherences via dynamical feedback, rather than deductive elimination of parses based on top-down constraints.
The connectionist model's behavior aligns with human data, indicating that dynamical, self-organizing mechanisms may address tractability problems in parsing.
papers.limitation:
The effect in the network simulation was somewhat unstable with longer training on the same materials and sometimes reversed itself.
Experiment 1 results could be explained by lexical automaticity (activation of compound senses in the lexicon) rather than syntactic parsing interference, though Experiment 2 addresses this.
future_direction: Further exploration of dynamical parsing models that use feedback and self-organization to handle incoherent structure representation.
Incorporating the problem of incoherent structure representation into the theory of grammar.
papers.abstract: Ungrammatical Inuences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing Whitney Tabor tabor@uconnvm.uconn.edu Bruno Galantucci Bruno.Galantucci@uconn.edu Department of Psychology University of Connecticut Storrs, CT 06269 USA Abstract A distinguishing feature of self-organizing models of cog- nitive structure is that they permit incompatible struc- tures to coexist at least temporarily. Here we report on a connectionist model of natural language process- ing which appears to temporarily construct incoherent structures. We then describe two reading-time studies which reveal people exhibiting the same tendency. In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: Attribution Analysis of Grammatical Dependencies in LSTMs
papers.research_question: Does the LSTM language model capture grammatical dependencies (subject-verb agreement) by using spurious correlations or by actually matching verbs with their subjects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LSTM language models enforce subject-verb agreement by identifying the subject noun, not by relying on spurious correlations, as demonstrated through layer-wise relevance propagation attribution analysis.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM language model enforces subject-verb agreement in an interpretable manner, and its success on the agreement task is not due to Clever Hans behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Model prediction accuracy on subject-verb agreement is positively correlated with its ability to assign higher relevance scores to the subject noun (N1) compared to other nouns (N2).
Determiners (The/the) adjust the magnitude and sometimes direction of the relevance introduced by nouns.
Polysemous verbs (like 'like') can bias the model and cause prediction errors.
For coordinated verb constructions (SVP and LVP), the model uses an alternative strategy that relies on verb coordination rather than solely identifying the subject.
The model fails on object relative clauses (ORC) and likely relies on Clever Hans behavior for that construction.
papers.limitation:
The work does not show that LSTMs can infer stack-like representations of hierarchical syntactic structure or memory-bounded approximations thereof.
The TSE templates are simple in terms of embedding depth and dependency length, limiting the complexity of the syntactic structures evaluated.
future_direction: Exploring whether LSTMs can infer hierarchical syntactic structure and handle more complex syntactic constructions.
papers.abstract: LSTM language models have been shown to capture syntax-sensitive grammatical dependencies such as subject-verb agreement with a high degree of accuracy (Linzen et al., 2016, inter alia). However, questions remain regarding whether they do so using spurious correlations, or whether they are truly able to match verbs with their subjects. This paper argues for the latter hypothesis. Using layer-wise relevance propagation (Bach et al., 2015), a technique that quantifies the contributions of input features to model behavior, we show that LSTM performance on number agreement is directly correlated with the model's ability to distinguish subjects from other nouns. Our results suggest that LSTM language models are able to infer robust representations of syntactic dependencies.

papers.title: Just-in-time and distributed task representations in language models
papers.research_question: When are transferrable task representations formed in language models during in-context learning, and how do they change over the context?
papers.core_contribution: Transferrable task representations in language models evolve non-monotonically and sporadically, activating only at key tokens, while a persistent representation of task identity is maintained throughout the context.
papers.conclusion: Language models form multiple types of task representations during in-context learning, with transferrable representations activating sporadically and task identity persisting, revealing a complex and nuanced dynamic of the model's internal state.
papers.key_findings:
Transferrable task representations (e.g., task vectors) accrue evidence from multiple in-context examples but form sporadically and non-monotonically.
Task identity representations are robustly decodable from residual activations across most tokens in the context, persisting throughout.
Transferrable task representations exhibit strong temporal locality, forming effectively only at specific tokens (e.g., the colon token before answer generation).
In longer- and mixed-generation tasks, transferrable task representations often decay over output units, showing semantic locality and limited task scope.
For complex tasks requiring state tracking or combining distinct subtasks, effective task representations are more distributed across tokens.
papers.limitation:
Zero-shot recontextualization remains challenging for tasks that require intermediate-state tracking or more complicated computation.
Overriding token activations at intermediate layers with task vectors may cause the model to lose task state information formed in earlier layers.
future_direction: Study the mechanistic bases for the strong temporal and scope locality observed in models' in-context transferrable task representations.
papers.abstract: Many of language models' impressive capabilities originate from their in-context learning: based on instructions or examples, they can infer and perform new tasks without weight updates. In this work, we investigate when representations for new tasks are formed in language models, and how these representations change over the course of context. We study two different task representations: those that are ''transferrable'' -- vector representations that can transfer task contexts to another model instance, even without the full prompt -- and simpler representations of high-level task categories. We show that transferrable task representations evolve in non-monotonic and sporadic ways, while task identity representations persist throughout the context. Specifically, transferrable task representations exhibit a two-fold locality. They successfully condense evidence when more examples are provided in the context. But this evidence accrual process exhibits strong temporal locality along the sequence dimension, coming online only at certain tokens -- despite task identity being reliably decodable throughout the context. In some cases, transferrable task representations also show semantic locality, capturing a small task ''scope'' such as an independent subtask. Language models thus represent new tasks on the fly through both an inert, sustained sensitivity to the task and an active, just-in-time representation to support inference.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language
papers.research_question: Do large language models have the ability to introspect about their internal linguistic knowledge, specifically grammatical knowledge and word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not exhibit introspection about their linguistic knowledge; their metalinguistic responses are not more aligned with their own internal probabilities than with those of similar models.
papers.conclusion: LLMs cannot introspect about their linguistic knowledge, and metalinguistic prompting should not be conflated with models' internal linguistic generalizations.
papers.key_findings:
Models achieve high accuracy on grammaticality and word prediction tasks under both direct (probability-based) and metalinguistic (prompt-based) evaluation methods.
The consistency between direct and metalinguistic evaluations is low (Cohen’s κ around 0.25).
There is no evidence of introspection: within-model alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations is not higher than cross-model alignment when controlling for model similarity.
Model similarity (both feature-based and empirical) predicts the alignment between metalinguistic and direct evaluations, but there is no additional 'same model effect'.
Larger models tend to have better performance on metalinguistic prompts and their metalinguistic responses are more correlated with direct evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested open-source models; closed-source models might behave differently.
The null result might be due to the specific tasks and models; introspection might emerge in other settings.
papers.abstract: There has been recent interest in whether large language models (LLMs) can introspect about their own internal states. Such abilities would make LLMs more interpretable, and also validate the use of standard introspective methods in linguistics to evaluate grammatical knowledge in models (e.g., asking "Is this sentence grammatical?"). We systematically investigate emergent introspection across 21 open-source LLMs, in two domains where introspection is of theoretical interest: grammatical knowledge and word prediction. Crucially, in both domains, a model's internal linguistic knowledge can be theoretically grounded in direct measurements of string probability. We then evaluate whether models' responses to metalinguistic prompts faithfully reflect their internal knowledge. We propose a new measure of introspection: the degree to which a model's prompted responses predict its own string probabilities, beyond what would be predicted by another model with nearly identical internal knowledge. While both metalinguistic prompting and probability comparisons lead to high task accuracy, we do not find evidence that LLMs have privileged "self-access". By using general tasks, controlling for model similarity, and evaluating a wide range of open-source models, we show that LLMs cannot introspect, and add new evidence to the argument that prompted responses should not be conflated with models' linguistic generalizations.

papers.title: Beyond Semantics: How Temporal Biases Shape Retrieval in Transformer and State-Space Models
papers.research_question: How do temporal biases shape information retrieval in transformer and state-space models during in-context learning, and how effectively can these models differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that both transformer and state-space models exhibit strong temporal biases (primacy and recency effects) in retrieving information, and in transformers, these biases are mechanistically linked to the function of induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Temporal biases are fundamental to in-context learning in both transformer and state-space architectures, shaping information retrieval in ways analogous to human episodic memory, with induction heads playing a key mechanistic role in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Both transformer and state-space models show a tendency for serial recall, predicting the token immediately following a repeated instance ('+1' token).
The strength of serial recall is modulated by the token's temporal position, showing strong primacy and recency effects, with model-specific biases (e.g., Mistral shows recency, Falcon-Mamba shows primacy).
Ablating induction heads in transformers significantly impairs both serial recall and the ability to selectively retrieve correct episodes in the presence of interference, confirming their causal role.
Despite architectural differences, state-space models exhibit comparable temporal biases to transformers, suggesting these biases arise from fundamental properties of sequential data processing.
Episodic retrieval is less reliable for memories embedded in the middle of a prompt, demonstrating a 'lost in the middle' effect even when semantic content is neutralized.
papers.limitation: The study primarily uses token-random prompts rather than natural text and analyzes next-token probabilities, representing a simplified information environment that isolates temporal effects from semantic confounds.
future_direction: Future work can explore the more complex interplay between 'when' something was said and 'what' was said in rich, semantic contexts.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is governed by both temporal and semantic relationships, shaping how Large Language Models (LLMs) retrieve contextual information. Analogous to human episodic memory, where the retrieval of specific events is enabled by separating events that happened at different times, this work probes the ability of various pretrained LLMs, including transformer and state-space models, to differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events. Specifically, we prompted models with sequences containing multiple presentations of the same token, which reappears at the sequence end. By fixing the positions of these repeated tokens and permuting all others, we removed semantic confounds and isolated temporal effects on next-token prediction. Across diverse sequences, models consistently placed the highest probabilities on tokens following a repeated token, but with a notable bias for those nearest the beginning or end of the input. An ablation experiment linked this phenomenon in transformers to induction heads. Extending the analysis to unique semantic contexts with partial overlap further demonstrated that memories embedded in the middle of a prompt are retrieved less reliably. Despite architectural differences, state-space and transformer models showed comparable temporal biases. Our findings deepen the understanding of temporal biases in in-context learning and offer an illustration of how these biases can enable temporal separation and episodic retrieval.

papers.title: Finding Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to humans, and how can such structures be identified?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation demonstrates that language models capture abstract linguistic structure similar to humans, and develops interpretability techniques to reveal this structure. It shows that models exhibit structural priming, generalize from indirect evidence, and that interpretability methods must be evaluated with care.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a detailed account of grammatical knowledge in language models and offers directions for using computational methods to investigate linguistic questions.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit human-like structural priming effects, indicating they capture abstract syntactic structure.
Language models can generalize linguistic patterns from indirect evidence, as shown by filtered corpus training experiments.
Interpretability methods for feature interaction detection vary in faithfulness and must be evaluated carefully.
Language models use monotonicity information to predict negative polarity item licensing.
Adjective order preferences in language models are influenced by data statistics and cognitive factors.
papers.abstract: When we speak, write or listen, we continuously make predictions based on our knowledge of a language's grammar. Remarkably, children acquire this grammatical knowledge within just a few years, enabling them to understand and generalise to novel constructions that have never been uttered before. Language models are powerful tools that create representations of language by incrementally predicting the next word in a sentence, and they have had a tremendous societal impact in recent years. The central research question of this thesis is whether these models possess a deep understanding of grammatical structure similar to that of humans. This question lies at the intersection of natural language processing, linguistics, and interpretability. To address it, we will develop novel interpretability techniques that enhance our understanding of the complex nature of large-scale language models. We approach our research question from three directions. First, we explore the presence of abstract linguistic information through structural priming, a key paradigm in psycholinguistics for uncovering grammatical structure in human language processing. Next, we examine various linguistic phenomena, such as adjective order and negative polarity items, and connect a model's comprehension of these phenomena to the data distribution on which it was trained. Finally, we introduce a controlled testbed for studying hierarchical structure in language models using various synthetic languages of increasing complexity and examine the role of feature interactions in modelling this structure. Our findings offer a detailed account of the grammatical knowledge embedded in language model representations and provide several directions for investigating fundamental linguistic questions using computational methods.

papers.title: What Syntactic Structures block Dependencies in RNN Language Models?
papers.research_question: Do RNN language models learn specific syntactic island constraints that block filler-gap dependencies, or are they merely sensitive to gross syntactic complexity?
papers.core_contribution: RNN language models learn fine-grained syntactic constraints for filler-gap dependencies, specifically island effects, and can maintain other dependencies like gender expectations through islands, indicating differentiated learning of syntactic rules.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on language modeling learn both the unbounded nature and specific constraints of filler-gap dependencies, separating different dependencies with fine-grained syntactic rules.
papers.key_findings:
RNN models maintain filler-gap dependencies through unbounded sentential embeddings, showing sensitivity to hierarchical structure.
Models attenuate expectations for gaps in island constructions but not for gender expectations, indicating island constraints are specific to filler-gap dependencies.
Models learn left branch islands and show gradient sensitivity to coordination islands, but fail to learn sentential subject islands.
The Google model shows unbounded dependency maintenance, while the Gulordava model shows some degradation with depth, reflecting human-like performance limitations.
Model behavior on coordination islands is un-humanlike, with some residual expectations for gaps.
papers.limitation:
Models are conspicuously un-humanlike in some performance characteristics, such as on coordination islands.
Models fail to learn sentential subject islands.
papers.abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) trained on a language modeling task have been shown to acquire a number of non-local grammatical dependencies with some success. Here, we provide new evidence that RNN language models are sensitive to hierarchical syntactic structure by investigating the filler--gap dependency and constraints on it, known as syntactic islands. Previous work is inconclusive about whether RNNs learn to attenuate their expectations for gaps in island constructions in particular or in any sufficiently complex syntactic environment. This paper gives new evidence for the former by providing control studies that have been lacking so far. We demonstrate that two state-of-the-art RNN models are are able to maintain the filler--gap dependency through unbounded sentential embeddings and are also sensitive to the hierarchical relationship between the filler and the gap. Next, we demonstrate that the models are able to maintain possessive pronoun gender expectations through island constructions---this control case rules out the possibility that island constructions block all information flow in these networks. We also evaluate three untested islands constraints: coordination islands, left branch islands, and sentential subject islands. Models are able to learn left branch islands and learn coordination islands gradiently, but fail to learn sentential subject islands. Through these controls and new tests, we provide evidence that model behavior is due to finer-grained expectations than gross syntactic complexity, but also that the models are conspicuously un-humanlike in some of their performance characteristics.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: Planning in a recurrent neural network that plays Sokoban
papers.research_question: How is planning internally represented and used in a recurrent neural network trained on Sokoban? Specifically, does the network causally represent a plan, how does the plan improve with computation, and why does it exhibit pacing behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The DRC recurrent neural network causally represents a plan for solving Sokoban puzzles, which improves with additional computation. The network exhibits pacing behavior to allocate more computation time for plan refinement, and its convolutional core can generalize to larger, out-of-distribution puzzles when combined with action probes.
papers.conclusion: The DRC model demonstrates interesting planning behaviors, making it a valuable model organism for studying learned planning in neural networks, with implications for understanding goal-oriented reasoning and AI alignment.
papers.key_findings:
The DRC maintains a causally represented plan that predicts future actions up to 50 steps ahead.
The plan's quality and length improve with more computation (thinking steps).
The DRC exhibits pacing behavior (cycles) to give itself extra computation time at the start of a level, which is incentivized by training.
Using action probes, the trained DRC can be extended to solve significantly larger, out-of-distribution Sokoban puzzles.
The DRC does not perform explicit search (generating and evaluating multiple plans) and shows low confidence in value representations.
papers.limitation:
The DRC does not perform explicit search by generating and evaluating multiple plans.
Causal interventions can cause naive deadlocks or fail to alter behavior when the plan is suboptimal.
The plan representation (box-directions probe) is incomplete, missing details like agent path planning and box ordering.
Some pacing cycles may be accidental rather than deliberate for plan refinement.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other models and tasks to uncover shared planning mechanisms.
Use the insights to detect and prevent goal misgeneralization in AI systems.
Investigate the conditions under which planning emerges in neural networks.
papers.abstract: Planning is essential for solving complex tasks, yet the internal mechanisms underlying planning in neural networks remain poorly understood. Building on prior work, we analyze a recurrent neural network (RNN) trained on Sokoban, a challenging puzzle requiring sequential, irreversible decisions. We find that the RNN has a causal plan representation which predicts its future actions about 50 steps in advance. The quality and length of the represented plan increases over the first few steps. We uncover a surprising behavior: the RNN "paces" in cycles to give itself extra computation at the start of a level, and show that this behavior is incentivized by training. Leveraging these insights, we extend the trained RNN to significantly larger, out-of-distribution Sokoban puzzles, demonstrating robust representations beyond the training regime. We open-source our model and code, and believe the neural network's interesting behavior makes it an excellent model organism to deepen our understanding of learned planning.

papers.title: Sharp Nearby, Fuzzy Far Away: How Neural Language Models Use Context
papers.research_question: How much context do neural language models use, how do they represent nearby versus long-range context, and how do copy mechanisms help in using context?
papers.core_contribution: LSTM language models use about 200 tokens of context, distinguish nearby and distant context (sensitive to word order only in nearby context), and rely on caching for copying distant words.
papers.conclusion: A standard LSTM language model can effectively use about 200 tokens of context, is sensitive to word order in nearby context but less so in long-range context, and relies on caches to copy words from far away.
papers.key_findings:
The LSTM language model has an effective context size of about 200 tokens.
The model is sensitive to word order in nearby context (within 50 tokens) but not in long-range context.
The model represents long-range context as a rough semantic field or topic.
The model can regenerate words from nearby context without a cache, but relies on a cache to copy words from long-range context.
The cache helps most for words that can only be copied from long-range context.
papers.limitation: Separating model behavior from language characteristics is challenging due to confounding factors like vocabulary size and dataset size.
future_direction: Experimenting with different model classes and languages
Investigating sentence-level interactions
papers.abstract: We know very little about how neural language models (LM) use prior linguistic context. In this paper, we investigate the role of context in an LSTM LM, through ablation studies. Specifically, we analyze the increase in perplexity when prior context words are shuffled, replaced, or dropped. On two standard datasets, Penn Treebank and WikiText-2, we find that the model is capable of using about 200 tokens of context on average, but sharply distinguishes nearby context (recent 50 tokens) from the distant history. The model is highly sensitive to the order of words within the most recent sentence, but ignores word order in the long-range context (beyond 50 tokens), suggesting the distant past is modeled only as a rough semantic field or topic. We further find that the neural caching model (Grave et al., 2017b) especially helps the LSTM to copy words from within this distant context. Overall, our analysis not only provides a better understanding of how neural LMs use their context, but also sheds light on recent success from cache-based models.

papers.title: State Design Matters: How Representations Shape Dynamic Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does inference-time state representation, along the axes of granularity (long-form trajectories versus summaries), structure (natural language versus symbolic encodings), and spatial grounding (text-only representations versus explicit spatial grounding via images or textual map encodings), affect performance on dynamic reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that design choices for representing state (granularity, structure, spatial grounding) are a decisive factor in performance on dynamic reasoning tasks, distinct from the availability of information itself.
papers.conclusion: State representation design matters as much as the information it contains; compact representations help when they preserve task-critical structure, but can be harmful if they omit necessary details. Future work should focus on verification and training for temporal spatial state tracking.
papers.key_findings:
Trajectory summarisation improves performance by reducing noise and stabilising long-horizon reasoning.
Natural language representations are the most robust across models.
Structured encodings help mainly for models with strong code or structured output priors.
Text-based spatial encodings (like Visualization-of-Thought) are most effective, primarily by inducing step-by-step spatial reasoning.
Even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons.
papers.limitation: Even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons, particularly when they must synthesise information to manage multiple subtasks to reach a goal.
future_direction: Pairing agents with verifiers during the process.
Training signals that directly encourage maintaining a consistent spatial state over many steps.
A shift toward dynamic evaluation to test true agentic competence.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) move from static reasoning tasks toward dynamic environments, their success depends on the ability to navigate and respond to an environment that changes as they interact at inference time. An underexplored factor in these settings is the representation of the state. Holding model parameters fixed, we systematically vary three key aspects: (1) state granularity (long form versus summary), (2) structure (natural language versus symbolic), and (3) spatial grounding (text-only versus images or textual map encodings) across sequential decision-making benchmarks. We find that trajectory summarisation improves performance by reducing noise and stabilising long-horizon reasoning. Second, natural language representations are the most robust across models, whereas structured encodings help mainly for models with strong code or structured output priors, such as JSON schemas. Third, while image-inputs show some benefit, text-based spatial encodings prove most effective. This advantage stems not from the spatial information itself, but from the act of construction, which compels the model to perform the spatial reasoning that static input does not elicit. Overall, we demonstrate that design choices for representing state are a decisive factor in performance, distinct from the availability of information itself. We note, however, that even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons, particularly when they must synthesise information to manage multiple subtasks to reach a goal.

papers.title: How Do Neural Sequence Models Generalize? Local and Global Context Cues for Out-of-Distribution Prediction
papers.research_question: After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its behavior be predicted? The paper investigates how neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts with conflicting local and global information.
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models generalize in out-of-distribution contexts by interpolating between local and global context predictions, and this interpolation can be modulated by noise-based regularization.
papers.conclusion: When neural sequence models are exposed to out-of-distribution contexts with conflicting local and global information, their behavior can be predicted and is best approximated by a log-linear interpolation of local and global predictors, with the weighting sometimes controllable by noise-based regularization.
papers.key_findings:
Neural LM predictions in surprising contexts are well approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global predictive distributions.
The relative strength of local versus global generalization varies across languages (e.g., local works better for English, global for Finnish and Chinese).
Input token noise (random substitution) encourages global generalization, while history representation noise (dropout) encourages local generalization.
A theoretical analysis shows that interpolation behavior arises in regularized log-linear models with separate local and global features.
papers.limitation: The theoretical explanation relies on a feature function that may not realistically represent deep network features, makes strong assumptions about feature predictive power, and becomes vacuous for certain parameter values.
future_direction: Explaining data-dependent aspects of the local-global trade-off, especially cross-linguistic differences not explained by typology.
Determining if architectural improvements can more effectively target specific kinds of structured generalization.
papers.abstract: After a neural sequence model encounters an unexpected token, can its behavior be predicted? We show that RNN and transformer language models exhibit structured, consistent generalization in out-of-distribution contexts. We begin by introducing two idealized models of generalization in next-word prediction: a local context model in which generalization is consistent with the last word observed, and a global context model in which generalization is consistent with the global structure of the input. In experiments in English, Finnish, Mandarin, and random regular languages, we demonstrate that neural language models interpolate between these two forms of generalization: their predictions are well-approximated by a log-linear combination of local and global predictive distributions. We then show that, in some languages, noise mediates the two forms of generalization: noise applied to input tokens encourages global generalization, while noise in history representations encourages local generalization. Finally, we offer a preliminary theoretical explanation of these results by proving that the observed interpolation behavior is expected in log-linear models with a particular feature correlation structure. These results help explain the effectiveness of two popular regularization schemes and show that aspects of sequence model generalization can be understood and controlled.

papers.title: Using Priming to Uncover the Organization of Syntactic Representations\n in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How are syntactic representations organized in neural language models? The paper investigates the organization of representations for sentences with relative clauses using a priming-based technique.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel technique based on syntactic priming to analyze how syntactic representations are organized in neural language models, and demonstrates that LSTM LMs' representations of sentences with relative clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner.
papers.conclusion: The proposed priming-based technique reveals that the representations of sentences with relative clauses in LSTM LMs are organized in a linguistically interpretable hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Sentences with the same syntactic structure are more similar to each other in the LM's representation space than lexically matched sentences with different structures.
Sentences with different types of relative clauses are more similar to each other than to sentences without relative clauses, suggesting LMs track the abstract property of a gap.
LMs track linguistically interpretable features like reduction and passivity, with passivity contributing more to similarity than reduction.
Similarity between sentences is driven not only by shared function words but also by abstract syntactic properties, though this ability decreases with increased training corpus size.
No evidence was found that the similarity between object RCs and other RCs predicts agreement prediction accuracy.
papers.limitation:
For linguistically interpretable classes without lexically observable properties, similarity might be driven by lexical items rather than abstract properties.
No evidence found that similarity between object RCs and other RCs predicts agreement prediction accuracy.
future_direction: Compare similarity matrices generated from LMs with human representations using priming experiments.
Explore how to bias models to track linguistically useful properties through architectural biases, training on auxiliary tasks, or data augmentation.
papers.abstract:
Neural language models (LMs) perform well on tasks that require sensitivity
to syntactic structure. Drawing on the syntactic priming paradigm from
psycholinguistics, we propose a novel technique to analyze the representations
that enable such success. By establishing a gradient similarity metric between
structures, this technique allows us to reconstruct the organization of the
LMs' syntactic representational space. We use this technique to demonstrate
that LSTM LMs' representations of different types of sentences with relative
clauses are organized hierarchically in a linguistically interpretable manner,
suggesting that the LMs track abstract properties of the sentence.

papers.title: Hierarchical Representation in Neural Language Models: Suppression and\n Recovery of Expectations
papers.research_question: Do neural language models induce hierarchical generalizations and use stack-like data structures for incremental word prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that neural language models can learn hierarchical generalizations and approximate stack-like data structures for suppressing and recovering expectations in syntactic structures, but recovery is imperfect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural language models can learn hierarchical generalizations and approximate stack-like behavior, but the recovery of expectations is imperfect, especially for deep structures.
papers.key_findings:
Models show ordering effects in center embedding sentences, indicating they can associate verbs with correct subjects in hierarchical structures.
Models can suppress and recover expectations for filler-gap dependencies across island constraints, but recovery is partial and weaker than in non-island contexts.
LSTM models sometimes perform better than the Transformer model on these syntactic tests despite having fewer parameters.
