Residual disentanglement yields four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning.
The isolated reasoning embedding accounts for unique variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and recruits visual regions beyond classical language areas.
The neural signature for reasoning peaks later (~350-400ms) than signals for lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with a processing hierarchy.
Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings are biased toward linguistically shallow features (lexicon, syntax), masking the contributions of deeper cognitive processing like reasoning.
The method provides a framework for mapping distinct cognitive functions from artificial models to the human brain.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on ECoG data provides limited spatial coverage, with insufficient sampling in frontal regions crucial for reasoning.
The role of layers beyond the reasoning saturation layer (around layer 30 in Qwen2.5-14B) remains unclear; they may encode more abstract representations.
future_direction: Integrate complementary modalities such as fMRI to improve spatial resolution.
Explore larger models optimized for multi-step reasoning to reveal stronger or more specialized reasoning signals.
Investigate how higher-level representations in deeper layers (beyond reasoning saturation) might align with cortical hierarchies or large-scale cognitive organization.
papers.abstract: Understanding how the human brain progresses from processing simple linguistic inputs to performing high-level reasoning is a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. While modern large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to model neural responses to language, their internal representations are highly "entangled," mixing information about lexicon, syntax, meaning, and reasoning. This entanglement biases conventional brain encoding analyses toward linguistically shallow features (e.g., lexicon and syntax), making it difficult to isolate the neural substrates of cognitively deeper processes. Here, we introduce a residual disentanglement method that computationally isolates these components. By first probing an LM to identify feature-specific layers, our method iteratively regresses out lower-level representations to produce four nearly orthogonal embeddings for lexicon, syntax, meaning, and, critically, reasoning. We used these disentangled embeddings to model intracranial (ECoG) brain recordings from neurosurgical patients listening to natural speech. We show that: 1) This isolated reasoning embedding exhibits unique predictive power, accounting for variance in neural activity not explained by other linguistic features and even extending to the recruitment of visual regions beyond classical language areas. 2) The neural signature for reasoning is temporally distinct, peaking later (~350-400ms) than signals related to lexicon, syntax, and meaning, consistent with its position atop a processing hierarchy. 3) Standard, non-disentangled LLM embeddings can be misleading, as their predictive success is primarily attributable to linguistically shallow features, masking the more subtle contributions of deeper cognitive processing.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Linear Mechanisms for Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether spatiotemporal reasoning in Vision Language Models (VLMs) can be explained by linear mechanisms (spatial IDs) that bind spatial/temporal information to object word activations, and how these mechanisms can be used to understand and improve VLMs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces spatial IDs, a linear mechanism by which VLMs bind spatial/temporal information to object word activations, and shows that these IDs causally mediate model beliefs and can be used to diagnose and improve VLMs.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that spatiotemporal IDs provide a linear mechanistic explanation for spatiotemporal reasoning in VLMs and offer ways to improve model design and diagnosis.
papers.key_findings:
VLMs encode object locations by linearly binding spatial IDs to textual activations.
Spatial IDs can causally mediate model beliefs about spatial relationships through interventions.
Spatial IDs reveal limitations in depth representation in VLMs.
Spatial IDs can diagnose failure modes in VLMs (e.g., vision encoder vs. crossmodal integration).
Analogous temporal IDs exist in video VLMs and similarly mediate temporal reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Limited to analyses in simple spatial queries or appearance-based temporal queries.
Only extract and steer models of sizes up to 14B parameters due to compute constraints.
Limited use cases for leveraging spatial IDs for VLM diagnostics or finetuning.
future_direction: Experimental design for more complex, open-ended queries.
Investigation into whether the spatial ID circuit plays a similarly prominent role in larger models.
Expanded use cases such as explicit temporal guidance at large scale.
papers.abstract: Spatio-temporal reasoning is a remarkable capability of Vision Language Models (VLMs), but the underlying mechanisms of such abilities remain largely opaque. We postulate that visual/geometrical and textual representations of spatial structure must be combined at some point in VLM computations. We search for such confluence, and ask whether the identified representation can causally explain aspects of input-output model behavior through a linear model. We show empirically that VLMs encode object locations by linearly binding \textit{spatial IDs} to textual activations, then perform reasoning via language tokens. Through rigorous causal interventions we demonstrate that these IDs, which are ubiquitous across the model, can systematically mediate model beliefs at intermediate VLM layers. Additionally, we find that spatial IDs serve as a diagnostic tool for identifying limitations in existing VLMs, and as a valuable learning signal. We extend our analysis to video VLMs and identify an analogous linear temporal ID mechanism. By characterizing our proposed spatiotemporal ID mechanism, we elucidate a previously underexplored internal reasoning process in VLMs, toward improved interpretability and the principled design of more aligned and capable models. We release our code for reproducibility: https://github.com/Raphoo/linear-mech-vlms.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: The Language Model Understood the Prompt was Ambiguous: Probing Syntactic Uncertainty Through Generation
papers.research_question: What is the extent of syntactic uncertainty in neural language models when processing temporary ambiguities, and how do disambiguating cues affect this uncertainty?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generation-based method to probe syntactic uncertainty in language models, finding that LMs maintain multiple interpretations during temporary ambiguities and are sensitive to disambiguating cues, though with some errors.
papers.conclusion: LMs exhibit syntactic uncertainty by considering multiple analyses simultaneously, and while they are generally sensitive to disambiguating cues, they sometimes show errors indicating lingering misinterpretations or difficulty with agreement cues.
papers.key_findings:
LMs exhibit uncertainty over temporary syntactic ambiguities, tracking multiple analyses in parallel.
The degree of bias varies across ambiguity types (NP/S, NP/Z, Noun/Verb) and specific sentences.
Disambiguating cues often appropriately reduce uncertainty in favor of the correct analysis.
For NP/Z ambiguities, some completions show confusion about sentence structure, indicating lingering effects of initial misinterpretations.
For Noun/Verb ambiguities, LMs sometimes fail to use number agreement cues correctly.
papers.limitation:
Relying on automatic classification of sentences can introduce noise due to parser errors.
Cannot automatically detect ungrammatical completions or those with unclear analysis.
future_direction: Determine whether inter-item variation in LMs' preferences mirrors human expectations and/or corpus statistics.
Overcome limitations in automatic classification and detection of ungrammatical sentences.
papers.abstract: Temporary syntactic ambiguities arise when the beginning of a sentence is compatible with multiple syntactic analyses. We inspect to which extent neural language models (LMs) exhibit uncertainty over such analyses when processing temporarily ambiguous inputs, and how that uncertainty is modulated by disambiguating cues. We probe the LM's expectations by generating from it: we use stochastic decoding to derive a set of sentence completions, and estimate the probability that the LM assigns to each interpretation based on the distribution of parses across completions. Unlike scoring-based methods for targeted syntactic evaluation, this technique makes it possible to explore completions that are not hypothesized in advance by the researcher. We apply this method to study the behavior of two LMs (GPT2 and an LSTM) on three types of temporary ambiguity, using materials from human sentence processing experiments. We find that LMs can track multiple analyses simultaneously; the degree of uncertainty varies across constructions and contexts. As a response to disambiguating cues, the LMs often select the correct interpretation, but occasional errors point to potential areas of improvement.

papers.title: You Do Not Fully Utilize Transformer's Representation Capacity
papers.research_question: How does the standard Transformer's reliance on the previous layer's hidden state lead to representation collapse, and can integrating representations from all previous layers mitigate this collapse and improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Layer-Integrated Memory (LIMe), a lightweight extension to Transformer attention that learns to route and integrate key-value representations from all previous layers, mitigating representation collapse and improving performance on language modeling and reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: LIMe mitigates representation collapse by distributing contextual information across layers via learned routing, improving performance without increasing hidden-state size.
papers.key_findings:
LIMe converges faster and achieves lower perplexity than standard Transformers.
LIMe improves accuracy on synthetic reasoning and arithmetic tasks by up to 30%.
LIMe preserves higher entropy and better token separability in value representations, mitigating collapse.
LIMe enables shallower models to match the performance of deeper baselines.
Analysis of learned routing weights shows systematic reuse of both local and long-distance features.
papers.limitation:
Additional communication between GPUs in pipeline parallel setup.
Vanilla implementation has O(L^2) asymptotic complexity.
future_direction: Exploration of width-depth trade-off in LIMe architectures.
Theoretical analysis of the routing mechanism.
papers.abstract: In contrast to RNNs, which compress their history into a single hidden state, Transformers can attend to all past tokens directly. However, standard Transformers rely solely on the hidden state from the previous layer to represent the entire context. We show that this design choice induces representation collapse and degrades performance. To address this issue, we introduce Layer-Integrated Memory (LIMe), a lightweight extension that leverages existing key-value buffers and learns per-head, per-layer routing weights to integrate representations from all previous layers with negligible overhead. Through extensive experiments-including language modeling, synthetic reasoning benchmarks, and very deep architectures-LIMe consistently achieves faster convergence, lower perplexity per FLOP, and substantial accuracy improvements on synthetic tasks while preserving higher value-vector entropy and improved token separability. Finally, our analysis of the learned routing weights reveals systematic reuse of both local and long-distance features, demonstrating how LIMe mitigates collapse, unlocks richer representations without increasing hidden-state size, and points to promising directions for future research.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Emergence and Effectiveness of Task Vectors in In-Context Learning: An Encoder Decoder Perspective
papers.research_question: How do transformers form task vectors during pretraining, and how does the quality of task encoding predict in-context learning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the task encoding-decoding framework and shows that transformers concurrently learn to encode latent tasks into separable representations and develop task-specific decoding algorithms during pretraining. It also introduces Task Decodability (TD) as a geometric measure that predicts in-context learning performance.
papers.conclusion: The task encoding-decoding framework provides a unifying perspective on how transformers perform in-context learning, with task decodability serving as a key predictor of performance.
papers.key_findings:
During training, task encoding and decoding emerge concurrently: as the model learns to separate representations by latent task, it also learns conditional decoding algorithms.
Task Decodability (TD) predicts ICL performance across tasks, model families, and scales.
Finetuning earlier layers improves task encoding and ICL performance more than finetuning later layers.
The quality of task encoding is causally related to ICL performance, as shown by activation patching interventions.
In-context examples, finetuning, and prompting all improve ICL performance by enhancing task encoding.
papers.limitation:
The experimental setup does not encompass tasks that require multi-step reasoning.
The TD metric requires careful design of task distribution to consist of semantically similar, confusing tasks.
future_direction: Extend the framework to tasks requiring multi-step reasoning.
Apply the findings to real-world tasks.
papers.abstract: Autoregressive transformers exhibit adaptive learning through in-context learning (ICL), which begs the question of how. Prior works have shown that transformers represent the ICL tasks as vectors in their representations. In this paper, we leverage the encoding-decoding framework to study how transformers form task vectors during pretraining and how their task encoding quality predicts ICL task performance. On synthetic ICL tasks, we analyze the training dynamics of a small transformer and report the coupled emergence of task encoding and decoding. As the model learns to encode different latent tasks (e.g., "Finding the first noun in a sentence.") into distinct, separable representations, it concurrently builds conditional decoding algorithms and improves its ICL performance. We validate this phenomenon across pretrained models of varying scales (Gemma-2 2B/9B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B) and over the course of pretraining in OLMo-7B. Further, we demonstrate that the quality of task encoding inferred from representations predicts ICL performance, and that, surprisingly, finetuning the earlier layers can improve the task encoding and performance more than finetuning the latter layers. Our empirical insights shed light into better understanding the success and failure modes of large language models via their representations.

papers.title: Understanding the learned look-ahead behavior of chess neural networks
papers.research_question: How do chess-playing neural networks implement look-ahead planning? Do they learn sophisticated planning algorithms or rely on pattern matching?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Leela chess model exhibits context-dependent look-ahead behavior up to seven moves, uses similar internal mechanisms for different future time steps, and considers multiple move sequences.
papers.conclusion: These results offer new insights into the emergence of sophisticated look-ahead capabilities in neural networks trained on strategic tasks, contributing to our understanding of AI reasoning in complex domains.
papers.key_findings:
The model's look-ahead behavior is highly context-dependent, varying significantly based on the specific chess position.
The model can process information about board states up to seven moves ahead.
The model processes 3rd, 5th, and 7th moves using similar internal mechanisms.
The model considers multiple possible move sequences rather than focusing on a single line of play.
Specific attention heads (e.g., L12H12) play crucial roles in moving information backward in time, especially in checkmate scenarios.
papers.limitation: The alternative move analysis is based on a limited sample size (around 600 puzzles) due to strict criteria.
papers.abstract: We investigate the look-ahead capabilities of chess-playing neural networks, specifically focusing on the Leela Chess Zero policy network. We build on the work of Jenner et al. (2024) by analyzing the model's ability to consider future moves and alternative sequences beyond the immediate next move. Our findings reveal that the network's look-ahead behavior is highly context-dependent, varying significantly based on the specific chess position. We demonstrate that the model can process information about board states up to seven moves ahead, utilizing similar internal mechanisms across different future time steps. Additionally, we provide evidence that the network considers multiple possible move sequences rather than focusing on a single line of play. These results offer new insights into the emergence of sophisticated look-ahead capabilities in neural networks trained on strategic tasks, contributing to our understanding of AI reasoning in complex domains. Our work also showcases the effectiveness of interpretability techniques in uncovering cognitive-like processes in artificial intelligence systems.

papers.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: To what extent do large language models (LLMs) reason via chain-of-thought prompting, and do they rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the PRONTO QA dataset and uses formal analysis to show that LLMs are capable of correct individual deduction steps but struggle with proof planning when multiple valid steps are available.
papers.conclusion: While the largest LLMs are generally capable of reasoning, they have difficulty with proof planning and selecting the correct proof step when multiple options are available.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are capable of making valid individual proof steps, even in fictional contexts.
LLMs have difficulty with proof planning: when multiple valid proof steps are available, they often select the wrong step, leading to incomplete proofs.
Real-world knowledge helps reasoning: performance is significantly better with true ontologies compared to fictional or false ones.
Longer proofs (5 hops) are challenging, especially with top-down traversal of the ontology.
For larger models, the main source of error is misleading steps rather than invalid steps.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to modus ponens, proof lengths of at most 5, and semantically simple sentences.
future_direction: Use PRONTO QA to compare LLM reasoning with human reasoning and explore which aspects of human reasoning LLMs acquired.
Develop reasoning systems with more sophisticated proof planning/search strategies, such as neurosymbolic approaches.
Investigate whether LLMs can produce longer proofs, reason with other deduction rules, or handle more semantically complex sentences.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable reasoning capabilities given chain-of-thought prompts (examples with intermediate reasoning steps). Existing benchmarks measure reasoning ability indirectly, by evaluating accuracy on downstream tasks such as mathematical reasoning. However, it is unclear how these models obtain the answers and whether they rely on simple heuristics rather than the generated chain-of-thought. To enable systematic exploration of the reasoning ability of LLMs, we present a new synthetic question-answering dataset called PrOntoQA, where each example is generated from a synthetic world model represented in first-order logic. This allows us to parse the generated chain-of-thought into symbolic proofs for formal analysis. Our analysis on InstructGPT and GPT-3 shows that LLMs are quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps, and so are generally capable of reasoning, even in fictional contexts. However, they have difficulty with proof planning: When multiple valid deduction steps are available, they are not able to systematically explore the different options.

papers.title: PILOT: Planning via Internalized Latent Optimization Trajectories for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we stabilize reasoning trajectories in compact LLMs by internalizing strategic planning from a teacher model, without relying on runtime external guidance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes PILOT, a non-invasive framework that uses a lightweight Hyper-Network to synthesize and inject query-conditioned latent guidance vectors into a frozen backbone model, internalizing strategic oversight to stabilize reasoning trajectories without modifying backbone weights.
papers.conclusion: PILOT effectively stabilizes single-path reasoning trajectories in LLMs by internalizing latent guidance, achieving consistent performance gains with minimal decoding overhead.
papers.key_findings:
PILOT consistently improves reasoning performance on mathematical and coding benchmarks (e.g., +8.9% on MATH500) with negligible inference latency overhead.
Latent anchoring via PILOT outperforms explicit textual planning methods, indicating an advantage to internalizing guidance over surface-form generation.
The optimal injection depth (pivot layer) for the latent anchor is task-dependent, with mathematics benefiting from deeper layers and code generation from shallower layers.
PILOT's energy-aligned injection mechanism prevents representation collapse ('embedding shock') and maintains the dispersion of the model's hidden states.
The method is parameter-efficient, adding only ~0.5% trainable parameters relative to the base model.
papers.limitation:
The Construct-and-Verify pipeline for data preparation introduces additional preprocessing complexity compared to standard supervised fine-tuning.
The optimal anchoring depth (pivot layer) is a domain-specific hyperparameter that requires empirical tuning for new tasks; a dynamic, instance-wise selection mechanism is not yet implemented.
future_direction: Developing a dynamic, instance-wise mechanism for selecting the optimal injection layer.
papers.abstract: Strategic planning is critical for multi-step reasoning, yet compact Large Language Models (LLMs) often lack the capacity to formulate global strategies, leading to error propagation in long-horizon tasks. Our analysis reveals that LLMs possess latent reasoning capabilities that can be unlocked when conditioned on explicit plans from a teacher model; however, runtime reliance on external guidance is often impractical due to latency and availability constraints. To bridge this gap, we propose PILOT (Planning via Internalized Latent Optimization Trajectories), a non-invasive framework designed to internalize the strategic oversight of large models into intrinsic Latent Guidance. Instead of altering backbone weights, PILOT employs a lightweight Hyper-Network to synthesize a query-conditioned Latent Guidance vector. This vector acts as an internal steering mechanism, guiding the model's representations toward optimal reasoning paths. Extensive experiments on mathematical and coding benchmarks demonstrate that PILOT effectively stabilizes reasoning trajectories, consistently outperforming strong baselines (e.g., +8.9% on MATH500) with negligible inference latency.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Learning Music Helps You Read: Using Transfer to Study Linguistic Structure in Language Models
papers.research_question: What kinds of abstract structural features do neural language models encode, and can these features be transferred to improve performance on natural language tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces TILT, a transfer learning method to analyze structural inductive biases in language models, and finds that LSTMs can transfer structural knowledge from non-linguistic data (music, code) and artificial languages to natural language, with transfer between human languages correlating with syntactic typological similarity.
papers.conclusion: LSTMs learn generalizable structural representations from various structured data, which can be transferred to model natural language; simple structural biases like head-dependent pairing are sufficient for this transfer, challenging the centrality of recursion.
papers.key_findings:
Training on non-linguistic structured data (MIDI music or Java code) improves zero-shot perplexity on Spanish compared to random baselines, indicating transfer of generalizable structural features.
Training on artificial languages with either hierarchical (nested) or flat (paired) token structure leads to similar substantial gains in modeling natural language, suggesting hierarchical recursion is not necessary for useful structural transfer.
Zero-shot transfer performance between natural languages is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity (WALS-syntax distance), even with zero vocabulary overlap.
Pretraining on a Zipfian random distribution provides minor improvement over a uniform random distribution, but far less than any structured data, indicating vocabulary distribution alone is insufficient for strong transfer.
papers.limitation:
The results are specific to LSTMs and may not generalize to Transformer architectures.
The typological distance metric (WALS-syntax) is based on only 49 features and may not be a perfectly accurate distance metric.
future_direction: Test if the results hold on Transformer architectures.
Ablate specific structural features by creating hypothetical languages that differ in single grammatical features.
Test with structured data that's completely unrelated to language, such as images.
papers.abstract: We propose transfer learning as a method for analyzing the encoding of grammatical structure in neural language models. We train LSTMs on non-linguistic data and evaluate their performance on natural language to assess which kinds of data induce generalizable structural features that LSTMs can use for natural language. We find that training on nonlinguistic data with latent structure (MIDI music or Java code) improves test performance on natural language, despite no overlap in surface form or vocabulary. To pinpoint the kinds of abstract structure that models may be encoding to lead to this improvement, we run similar experiments with two artificial parentheses languages: one which has a hierarchical recursive structure, and a control which has paired tokens but no recursion. Surprisingly, training a model on either of these artificial languages leads to the same substantial gains when testing on natural language. Further experiments on transfer between natural languages controlling for vocabulary overlap show that zeroshot performance on a test language is highly correlated with typological syntactic similarity to the training language, suggesting that representations induced by pre-training correspond to the cross-linguistic syntactic properties. Our results provide insights into the ways that neural models represent abstract syntactic structure, and also about the kind of structural inductive biases which allow for natural language acquisition.

papers.title: Interpreting Emergent Planning in Model-Free Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: Can model-free reinforcement learning agents learn to perform decision-time planning internally?
papers.core_contribution: Provides the first mechanistic evidence that model-free RL agents can learn to plan internally, and introduces a concept-based interpretability procedure for investigating planning in such agents.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that model-free RL agents can learn to internally plan, and that the learned planning algorithm resembles bidirectional search, which is efficient for Sokoban.
papers.key_findings:
The DRC agent linearly represents planning-relevant concepts (Agent Approach Direction and Box Push Direction) in its ConvLSTM cell states, as shown by high probe accuracy.
The agent forms internal plans iteratively, using a process resembling parallelized bidirectional search, and refines plans with additional test-time compute.
Interventions on the agent's concept representations can steer its behavior, demonstrating that the plans causally influence action selection.
The planning capability emerges during training and coincides with the emergence of planning-like behavior such as benefiting from extra test-time compute.
Preliminary evidence suggests that similar planning mechanisms can be found in other architectures (ResNet) and environments (Mini PacMan).
papers.limitation:
The analysis is specific to Sokoban and a single agent architecture.
The methodology relies on having a good hypothesis for what concepts the agent might be using to plan.
The interventions are somewhat crude.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to other environments and agents.
Investigate whether similar planning mechanisms emerge in large language models trained with RL.
papers.abstract: We present the first mechanistic evidence that model-free reinforcement learning agents can learn to plan. This is achieved by applying a methodology based on concept-based interpretability to a model-free agent in Sokoban -- a commonly used benchmark for studying planning. Specifically, we demonstrate that DRC, a generic model-free agent introduced by Guez et al. (2019), uses learned concept representations to internally formulate plans that both predict the long-term effects of actions on the environment and influence action selection. Our methodology involves: (1) probing for planning-relevant concepts, (2) investigating plan formation within the agent's representations, and (3) verifying that discovered plans (in the agent's representations) have a causal effect on the agent's behavior through interventions. We also show that the emergence of these plans coincides with the emergence of a planning-like property: the ability to benefit from additional test-time compute. Finally, we perform a qualitative analysis of the planning algorithm learned by the agent and discover a strong resemblance to parallelized bidirectional search. Our findings advance understanding of the internal mechanisms underlying planning behavior in agents, which is important given the recent trend of emergent planning and reasoning capabilities in LLMs through RL

papers.title: Representation of Word Meaning in the Intermediate Projection Layer of a Neural Language Model
papers.research_question: How does an LSTM language model represent high-level lexico-semantic information, and how does this compare to human semantic knowledge and brain imaging data?
papers.core_contribution: LSTM language models encode lexical semantic knowledge in their activation patterns, which correlates with human similarity judgments and brain imaging data.
papers.conclusion: LSTM language models not only encode syntactic knowledge but also represent semantic content in a way consistent with human conceptual knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Similarities between model vectors predict human similarity judgments, with stronger correlation for semantic similarity than relatedness.
Semantic features are more decodable from model representations before the target word than after it.
Model representations correlate with brain imaging data, indicating alignment with human cognitive representations.
papers.abstract: Performance in language modelling has been significantly improved by training recurrent neural networks on large corpora. This progress has come at the cost of interpretability and an understanding of how these architectures function, making principled development of better language models more difficult. We look inside a state-of-the-art neural language model to analyse how this model represents high-level lexico-semantic information.

papers.title: Addressing Some Limitations of Transformers with Feedback Memory
papers.research_question: How can we address the limitations of Transformers in accessing long memory and updating state for sequential tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The Feedback Transformer architecture exposes all previous representations to all future representations, enabling shallow models to achieve strong performance on sequential tasks.
papers.conclusion: The Feedback Transformer addresses fundamental limitations of Transformers in sequential processing, offering a more efficient and powerful architecture for autoregressive tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Feedback Transformer outperforms standard Transformers on tasks requiring long memory and state updates, such as algorithmic tasks and reinforcement learning.
Feedback Transformer achieves comparable or better performance with smaller, shallower models, leading to faster inference speeds.
The architecture reduces memory footprint and computational cost through shared key-value projections.
Feedback Transformer matches state-of-the-art language modeling results with models half the size of baselines.
The model demonstrates improved ability to track and update internal state over long sequences.
papers.abstract: Transformers have been successfully applied to sequential, auto-regressive tasks despite being feedforward networks. Unlike recurrent neural networks, Transformers use attention to capture temporal relations while processing input tokens in parallel. While this parallelization makes them computationally efficient, it restricts the model from fully exploiting the sequential nature of the input. The representation at a given layer can only access representations from lower layers, rather than the higher level representations already available. In this work, we propose the Feedback Transformer architecture that exposes all previous representations to all future representations, meaning the lowest representation of the current timestep is formed from the highest-level abstract representation of the past. We demonstrate on a variety of benchmarks in language modeling, machine translation, and reinforcement learning that the increased representation capacity can create small, shallow models with much stronger performance than comparable Transformers.

papers.title: Are Neural Networks Extracting Linguistic Properties or Memorizing Training Data? An Observation with a Multilingual Probe for Predicting Tense
papers.research_question: Does BERT extract abstract linguistic properties or memorize shallow patterns from training data, as evaluated through a multilingual tense prediction probe?
papers.core_contribution: BERT appears to memorize shallow, lexically-marked patterns from training data rather than learning abstract linguistic representations, as evidenced by a large performance gap in tense prediction between French (morphologically marked) and Chinese (requiring abstract inference).
papers.conclusion: BERT is more likely to memorize shallow patterns from the training set than to uncover abstract linguistic properties, and contrasting linguistic probes across languages is a valuable research direction.
papers.key_findings:
BERT achieves high tense prediction accuracy for French (where tense is morphologically marked) but performance drops sharply for Chinese (where tense is inferred from lexical, syntactic, and pragmatic cues).
Model performance decreases as test sentences become less similar to training sentences, indicating reliance on memorization rather than generalization.
A multilingual probing setup helps avoid the confounder of the probe learning the task instead of the representation.
Handcrafted feature-based SVM (featSVM) validates the theoretical relevance of designed features for Chinese tense prediction.
Fine-tuning BERT (fineBert) yields the best performance, but the gap between languages remains.
papers.limitation: The performance difference between French and Chinese could be due to confounders such as training set size or model architecture, though the authors argue similar XNLI performance mitigates this.
future_direction: Extending the multilingual probe approach to other languages and linguistic properties.
papers.abstract: We evaluate the ability of Bert embeddings to represent tense information, taking French and Chinese as a case study. In French, the tense information is expressed by verb morphology and can be captured by simple surface information. On the contrary, tense interpretation in Chinese is driven by abstract, lexical, syntactic and even pragmatic information. We show that while French tenses can easily be predicted from sentence representations, results drop sharply for Chinese, which suggests that

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: Spectral Journey: How Transformers Predict the Shortest Path
papers.research_question: Can decoder-only transformer language models learn to predict shortest paths on simple graphs, and what algorithm do they learn internally?
papers.core_contribution: Two-layer decoder-only transformers can learn to predict shortest paths on simple graphs, and mechanistic analysis reveals they learn a spectral embedding correlated with the line graph Laplacian, leading to the novel Spectral Line Navigation algorithm.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that 2-layer decoder-only transformers can learn shortest path prediction with high accuracy, and by analyzing attention dynamics and embeddings, they propose the Spectral Line Navigation algorithm, which is derived from the spectral decomposition of the line graph.
papers.key_findings:
Two-layer decoder-only transformer models can learn to predict shortest paths on simple, connected graphs containing up to 10 nodes.
Models learn attention heads that attend to edges containing the current node and the target node when selecting the next edge in the path.
The model's edge embeddings after the first layer are highly correlated with the spectral decomposition of the line graph Laplacian.
Increasing the number of attention heads improves accuracy and robustness, especially when there are many near-optimal paths.
Based on the mechanistic insights, a novel approximate path-finding algorithm, Spectral Line Navigation (SLN), is proposed and achieves 99.32% accuracy on the test set.
papers.limitation:
The causal mask prevents the model's edge embeddings from perfectly matching the line graph decomposition because future edges cannot be attended to.
The study is limited to decoder-only architectures; encoder-decoder models might perform better but are not explored.
future_direction: Exploring graph tasks beyond shortest path prediction.
Investigating the trade-off between model size and graph size.
Studying alternative forms of generalization beyond unseen graph structures.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only transformers lead to a step-change in capability of large language models. However, opinions are mixed as to whether they are really planning or reasoning. A path to making progress in this direction is to study the model's behavior in a setting with carefully controlled data. Then interpret the learned representations and reverse-engineer the computation performed internally. We study decoder-only transformer language models trained from scratch to predict shortest paths on simple, connected and undirected graphs. In this setting, the representations and the dynamics learned by the model are interpretable. We present three major results: (1) Two-layer decoder-only language models can learn to predict shortest paths on simple, connected graphs containing up to 10 nodes. (2) Models learn a graph embedding that is correlated with the spectral decomposition of the line graph. (3) Following the insights, we discover a novel approximate path-finding algorithm Spectral Line Navigator (SLN) that finds shortest path by greedily selecting nodes in the space of spectral embedding of the line graph.

papers.title: RECALL: Library-Like Behavior In Language Models is Enhanced by Self-Referencing Causal Cycles
papers.research_question: How can self-referencing causal cycles (RECALL) mitigate the reversal curse in autoregressive language models, enabling them to recall preceding context from succeeding tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces self-referencing causal cycles (RECALL) as a natural mechanism in pretraining data that enables autoregressive language models to bypass the reversal curse, and proposes a two-step prompting strategy to leverage it for reliable information retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Self-referencing causal cycles (RECALL) provide a natural mechanism for language models to overcome the reversal curse, and leveraging these cycles through prompting can improve the reliability of responses to prompts affected by the curse.
papers.key_findings:
RECALL enables models to recall preceding tokens from succeeding ones through cycle tokens, which create self-referencing causal cycles.
Cycle tokens act as hyperlinks in pretraining data, allowing models to bridge distant parts of text.
A two-step RECALL-aware prompting strategy (recollect context, then utilize it) effectively resolves the preceding line problem in key writings.
RECALL works under stochastic conditions with candidate sets, with accuracy inversely proportional to candidate set size.
The reversal curse can be mitigated without architectural changes or data augmentation by leveraging naturally occurring cycles.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted in controlled settings with simplified token sequences.
Real-world performance may be influenced by additional factors such as retrieval-augmented generation or web search.
Further interpretability techniques may be required to precisely attribute parametric information retrieval to specific cycle tokens.
Larger models often utilize fully or partially closed-source training data, making extraction of pretraining data difficult.
papers.abstract: We introduce the concept of the self-referencing causal cycle (abbreviated RECALL) - a mechanism that enables large language models (LLMs) to bypass the limitations of unidirectional causality, which underlies a phenomenon known as the reversal curse. When an LLM is prompted with sequential data, it often fails to recall preceding context. For example, when we ask an LLM to recall the line preceding "O say does that star-spangled banner yet wave" in the U.S. National Anthem, it often fails to correctly return "Gave proof through the night that our flag was still there" - this is due to the reversal curse. It occurs because language models such as ChatGPT and Llama generate text based on preceding tokens, requiring facts to be learned and reproduced in a consistent token order. While the reversal curse is often viewed as a limitation, we offer evidence of an alternative view: it is not always an obstacle in practice. We find that RECALL is driven by what we designate as cycle tokens - sequences that connect different parts of the training data, enabling recall of preceding tokens from succeeding ones. Through rigorous probabilistic formalization and controlled experiments, we demonstrate how the cycles they induce influence a model's ability to reproduce information. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide our code and experimental details at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/remember-B0B8/.

papers.title: When Can Transformers Ground and Compose: Insights from Compositional Generalization Benchmarks
papers.research_question: When and how can transformer models ground language to a visual world and compose object attributes to solve compositional generalization tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Simple transformer-based models (GroCoT) can achieve strong compositional generalization on grounded navigation tasks, with the main challenge being target identification. A simpler task (RefEx) reveals that even a single self-attention layer can ground and compose attributes, and its computations can be fully interpreted.
papers.conclusion: Transformer models are capable of grounded compositional generalization, and their success can be understood through analysis of their attention mechanisms, as demonstrated on both complex benchmarks and a simplified interpretable task.
papers.key_findings:
GroCoT, a simple transformer-based model, outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and GSRR benchmarks.
The primary difficulty in ReaSCAN is target identification, not navigation or sequence generation.
The C2 test split in ReaSCAN is unfair; with a corrected setup, transformers can generalize to deeper command structures.
A one-layer, one-head attention-only transformer can solve the RefEx task and generalize to novel compositions of object attributes.
The computations of the attention-only transformer on RefEx can be fully described via a precise mathematical construction of its learned parameters.
papers.abstract: Humans can reason compositionally whilst grounding language utterances to the real world. Recent benchmarks like ReaSCAN (Wu et al., 2021) use navigation tasks grounded in a grid world to assess whether neural models exhibit similar capabilities. In this work, we present a simple transformer-based model that outperforms specialized architectures on ReaSCAN and a modified version (Qiu et al., 2021) of gSCAN (Ruis et al., 2020). On analyzing the task, we find that identifying the target location in the grid world is the main challenge for the models. Furthermore, we show that a particular split in ReaSCAN, which tests depth generalization, is unfair. On an amended version of this split, we show that transformers can generalize to deeper input structures. Finally, we design a simpler grounded compositional generalization task, RefEx, to investigate how transformers reason compositionally. We show that a single self-attention layer with a single head generalizes to novel combinations of object attributes. Moreover, we derive a precise mathematical construction of the transformer’s computations from the learned network. Overall, we provide valuable insights about the grounded compositional generalization task and the behaviour of transformers on it, which would be useful for researchers working in this area.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: Do Language Models Understand Anything? On the Ability of LSTMs to Understand Negative Polarity Items
papers.research_question: Does an LSTM language model understand the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and can it detect the scope of the licensing context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that an LSTM language model can detect the relationship between negative polarity items and their licensing contexts, and that the model's hidden representations encode information about the scope of the licensing context.
papers.conclusion: The LSTM model is capable of handling NPI constructions and the licensing signal can be extracted from its hidden representations, paving the way for linking linguistic theory to neural models.
papers.key_findings:
The model assigns lower perplexity to sentences with correct NPI licensing compared to ungrammatical counterparts.
The model shows a strong preference for NPIs in negative contexts over positive contexts.
The model's hidden states can be used to predict the scope of the licensing context with high accuracy.
The model outperforms a baseline using GloVe embeddings in scope detection.
The effect of distance between NPI and licensing context: the model's performance degrades with longer distances.
papers.limitation:
The model's ability to handle NPI constructions degrades with longer distances between the NPI and the licensing context.
The study is limited to a subset of NPIs (those licensed by negative operators) and does not cover the full diversity of NPI constructions.
future_direction: Investigate a wider typological range of NPI constructions
Compare model performance with human judgments
Design entailment tasks based on linguistic hypotheses about NPI licensing
papers.abstract: In this paper, we attempt to link the inner workings of a neural language model to linguistic theory, focusing on a complex phenomenon well discussed in formal linguistics: (negative) polarity items. We briefly discuss the leading hypotheses about the licensing contexts that allow negative polarity items and evaluate to what extent a neural language model has the ability to correctly process a subset of such constructions. We show that the model finds a relation between the licensing context and the negative polarity item and appears to be aware of the scope of this context, which we extract from a parse tree of the sentence. With this research, we hope to pave the way for other studies linking formal linguistics to deep learning.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like the Brain? Sentence-Level Evidences from Layer-Wise Embeddings and fMRI
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the similarity between LLM representations and human brain activity is due to model scaling or deeper alignment with human language processing principles.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that instruction tuning and semantic comprehension ability, rather than model scale alone, drive the alignment between LLM representations and human brain activity during sentence processing.
papers.conclusion: Instruction tuning and semantic comprehension capacity, not merely parameter size, are key drivers of neural similarity, and the alignment is anatomically and functionally specific to intermediate layers and hemispheric specializations.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers of LLMs show higher correlation with brain activity than final layers.
Instruction-tuned models exhibit better performance and stronger neural alignment compared to their base versions.
Hemispheric asymmetry in brain regions aligns with functional specialization, with left-hemisphere regions correlating more with core language processing and right-hemisphere regions with higher cognitive functions.
future_direction: Training procedures that explicitly target alignment with brain data to produce more cognitively plausible models.
Developing hybrid neuro-symbolic LLMs to better reflect distributed and lateralized processing patterns observed in the brain.
papers.abstract: Understanding whether large language models (LLMs) and the human brain converge on similar computational principles remains a fundamental and important question in cognitive neuroscience and AI. Do the brain-like patterns observed in LLMs emerge simply from scaling, or do they reflect deeper alignment with the architecture of human language processing? This study focuses on the sentence-level neural mechanisms of language models, systematically investigating how layer-wise representations in LLMs align with the dynamic neural responses during human sentence comprehension. By comparing hierarchical embeddings from 14 publicly available LLMs with fMRI data collected from participants, who were exposed to a naturalistic narrative story, we constructed sentence-level neural prediction models to identify the model layers most significantly correlated with brain region activations. Results show that improvements in model performance drive the evolution of representational architectures toward brain-like hierarchies, particularly achieving stronger functional and anatomical correspondence at higher semantic abstraction levels. These findings advance our understanding of the computational parallels between LLMs and the human brain, highlighting the potential of LLMs as models for human language processing.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses.
